query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, sustained loading causes a strain‐induced breakdown of interfacial short-range order (SRO), which facilitates increased dislocation transmission across the phase boundaries and thereby accelerates creep deformations.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coatings with alternating FCC and BCC phases that initially exhibit a uniform interfacial chemical ordering.
generation.intervention: Systematically tune the interfacial characteristics by varying layer thickness and the degree of interfacial mixing/coherency to modulate the stability of SRO at the interfaces.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under sustained loading (creep conditions) at elevated temperatures and stress levels, while retaining the multilayer architecture.
generation.structural_mediator: The condition of the interfacial SRO (intact versus disrupted) that directly mediates dislocation nucleation and glide at the FCC/BCC boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained stress, localized mechanical loading disrupts the interfacial SRO. This disruption reduces local resistance to dislocation motion, thereby increasing dislocation transmission across the interface and leading to enhanced progressive plastic deformation (creep).
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with intentionally weakened SRO at the interfaces (via increased interfacial mixing or reduced layer thickness) will display higher creep rates and a more homogeneous distribution of plastic strain compared to baseline multilayers with intact interfacial SRO.
generation.baseline: Multilayer samples with unmodified interfacial properties that maintain a robust SRO, exhibiting lower creep rates and relatively more localized deformation mechanisms.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to hold within the regime where the multilayer structure is preserved and under stress/temperature conditions that do not trigger alternative phase transformations or deformation modes beyond SRO-mediated dislocation processes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold levels of interfacial SRO breakdown and the quantitative relationship between SRO disruption and creep rate remain to be established, and may be influenced by other factors such as overall lattice distortion and local compositional fluctuations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA multilayer samples with systematically varied interfacial mixing (e.g., by altering layer thickness and annealing conditions) to intentionally modify the degree of SRO. Subject these samples to sustained creep testing at controlled elevated temperatures and stresses.
measurements: Characterize interfacial SRO and dislocation structures using high-resolution TEM and energy-filtered 4D-STEM.
Quantify dislocation density and distribution across layers before and after creep tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exhibiting engineered disruption of interfacial SRO do not show significantly higher creep rates or increased dislocation transmission relative to those with preserved SRO, then the hypothesis that interfacial SRO breakdown governs enhanced plastic deformation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, nanoscale small-volume materials typically exhibit high strength but low tensile ductility. The latter is particularly important for the structural reliability of many micro/nanodevices. Here, we have achieved unusual room-temperature tensile ductility in excess of 100% under a high tensile flow stress in single-crystalline <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi HEA nanopillars. Our experimental, computational, and theoretical investigations showed that the ultrahigh uniform tensile ductility was caused by the intensive activation of distinct twinning mechanisms (nucleation, interaction, propagation, and coalescence of nanotwins) and extensive twin-dislocation interactions. These unique plasticity mechanisms originate from the atomic-level chemical complexity of the HEA that generates variable local SFEs and further synergistically coordinates a spatial activation of a series of deformation mechanisms. Our findings provide mechanistic insights for understanding plastic deformations of small-volume metallic materials and create a mechanistic map enabling the design of micro/nanodevices with reliable mechanical and functional properties. High or medium- entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) are multi-principal element alloys with equal atomic elemental composition, some of which have shown record-breaking mechanical performance. However, the link between short-range order (SRO) and the exceptional mechanical properties of these alloys has remained elusive. The local destruction of SRO by dislocation glide has been predicted to lead to a rejuvenated state with increased entropy and free energy, creating softer zones within the matrix and planar fault boundaries that enhance the ductility, but this has not been verified. Here, we integrate in situ nanomechanical testing with energy-filtered four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) and directly observe the rejuvenation during cyclic mechanical loading in single crystal CrCoNi at room temperature. Surprisingly, stacking faults (SFs) and twin boundaries (TBs) are reversible in initial cycles but become irreversible after a thousand cycles, indicating SF energy reduction and rejuvenation. The frequent changes of atom type and size cause a large atomic-scale lattice distortion in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), resulting in excellent mechanical properties, such as great strength and good ductility (), and high fracture toughness (, ). In particular, refractory MPEA (RMPEA) shows high strength at elevated temperatures (), but its low room-temperature ductility hinders the wide applications (). Recently, non-screw dislocation slip plays an important contribution to plastic deformation in RMPEA () and attracts a lot of great attention to break through this dilemma (). Additionally, the differences of the electronic interactions lead to the existence of preference or avoidance in the atom bonding and then produce chemical short-range order (SRO) to reduce the free energy of the system confirmed by experiments (). Regions with stronger chemical ordering can locally accommodate size differences more efficiently, reducing lattice distortion, whereas regions with weaker or frustrated ordering amplify local strains. This reciprocal interplay governs the heterogeneity of the atomic-scale strain field, providing a fundamental basis for the tunable Hookean and non-Hookean superelasticity observed in the (TiZrHf)50Ni50-xCox alloys. By adjusting the Ni/Co ratio, the balance between chemical ordering and lattice distortion can be finely controlled, resulting in a continuous strain-field landscape that can be precisely tuned through minor compositional variations (<2 at.%), unlike binary or ternary systems where similar adjustments often induce discrete phase transitions. The chemical complexity of the high-entropy system facilitates smooth evolution between strain states, enabling continuous modulation of the elastic response— from Hookean to non-Hookean and back to Hookean—within a single alloy system. Such compositional tuning of elasticity has not been achieved in conventional alloys.

In our HEA, SRO clusters have similar elemental concentrations and the same crystal structures as the HEA matrix. For example, FCCP, IND, and BCCP are SRO clusters that have similar elemental concentrations and the same FCC crystal structure. On the other hand, the crystal structure and chemical composition of a nanoscale precipitate in a HEA are well defined and generally differ from those of the HEA matrix. Hence, we do not consider the SRO clusters as precipitates. In the present CoCuFeNiPd HEA study, we demonstrated that SRO can lead to the formation of a pseudo-composite microstructure of BCCP, IND, and FCCP structures. decision.trend: Early studies in HEAs focused on identifying how dislocation slip, twinning, and phase transformations govern deformation in relatively homogeneous materials. Later work uncovered that under strain, HEAs can develop mechanically induced short‐range order (MSRO) or even experience a 'rejuvenation' of local atomic configurations, which alters dislocation activity. Meanwhile, simulation work on creep in high‐entropy (super)alloys has highlighted stress–temperature effects and the role of interfacial phenomena. This progression indicates a shift from a global view of dislocation-based mechanisms toward understanding how local chemical ordering and interfaces modify plasticity.
decision.unsolved: For FCC/BCC HEA multilayers, it remains unresolved how the nanoscale multilayer architecture—with its inherent compositional complexity, lattice distortions, and short-range order at interfaces—affects the local breakdown or reconfiguration of SRO and the ensuing dislocation dynamics under sustained (creep) loading. In particular, the way in which the interfaces mediate progressive plastic deformation, and under which conditions different mechanisms dominate, is still unclear.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the interfacial characteristics (for example, by tuning layer thickness and degree of interfacial mixing/coherency) to control the extent of local SRO disruption and dislocation transmission across the FCC/BCC boundaries.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend of recent studies that link strain-induced changes in local chemical order and defect interactions to mechanical performance. By deliberately altering interfacial structures—a key feature of the multilayer design—the experiment can test whether localized breakdown of SRO at the interfaces is the governor of creep behavior, providing a controlled comparison that addresses the unique cues of compositional complexity and lattice distortions in HEA multilayers.
